title: Diversarum hereseon liber
author: Philastrius
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0122a.stoa001.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's CSEL and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Quem Hermes ille uanus paganus Trismegistus docuit post deum omnipotentem non alium nisi solem debere ipsum et homines adorare; qui cum ad Celtarum prouinciam perrexisset, ipse eos dinoscitur docuisse, atque huic errori ut succumberent isdem suasisse. Quem solem Iudaei captiuati adorabant, ut Hiezechiel propheta eosdem Iudaeos incusando condemnat, ac reos criminis maiestatis declarat et arguit contestando, sicut scriptum est.
passages.english: Hermes Trismegistus, that empty-headed pagan, taught that after almighty God both he himself and [all] men ought to worship none other than the sun; and when he had travelled to the province of the Celts, he is known to have taught them [this] and to have persuaded them to give way to this error. The Jews in captivity worshipped this sun, as the prophet Ezekiel condemns those same Jews in accusing them, and declares them guilty of the crime of treason [against God's majesty] and convicts them by bearing witness [against them], as it is written.
passages.notes: The opening 'Quem' refers to an antecedent (a heresy) in the preceding text, which is not supplied; it is rendered loosely. 'ipsum et homines' is awkward; it may mean 'he himself and [other] men'.

passages.original: Aeonas autem nuntians sicut Marcion delirauit. Qui etiam generationem hominum execratur, et ius nuptiarum legitimum abicit, idque iuris a deo statutum non confitetur.
passages.english: And announcing aeons, he raved like Marcion. He also curses the begetting of human beings, and rejects the lawful right of marriage, and does not acknowledge that this right was established by God.
passages.notes: The subject ("he") is not named within the passage; it refers to a heretic described in the preceding text. Linking aeons with Marcion is unusual, since aeons are more typically Valentinian, but the text reads so.

passages.original: Alia est heresis quae secundum paganorum uanitatem siderum diuersa nomina profitetur, ut Hermes ille Trismegistus, qui uanus potius quam magnus iudicandus est, et poetae quidam ei consimiles, qui cometas et pogonias et Hyadas, Haedos, et alia huiusmodi adserunt nomine delirantes, cum scriptura pauca nomina siderum nobis edixerit dicente Iob beato propheta, ante quam pagani e sanctis scripturis siderum nomina transtulissent.
passages.english: There is another heresy which, following the emptiness of the pagans, professes various names of the stars, like that Hermes Trismegistus, who ought to be judged empty rather than great, and certain poets like him, who in their raving assert by name comets and bearded stars and the Hyades, the Kids, and other things of this kind, although Scripture has declared to us a few names of stars, when the blessed prophet Job speaks, before the pagans had carried over the names of the stars from the holy Scriptures.
passages.notes: 'pogonias': 'bearded' comets (Greek pōgōnias). There is a play on Trismegistus, 'thrice-greatest', and 'empty rather than great'.

passages.original: Pagani autem post Iudaeos siue a pago, id est loco, siue prouincia una dicti sunt siue Pagano rege, quod uerum esse, ut ait Hesiodus Grecus poeta, manifestatum est. Si ergo a pago, loci est indicium, sicuti et nunc dicitur (de pago illo\': si autem de idolis, *** quod ea colentes sculptilia ita nominabantur pagani, id est gentiles.
passages.english: After the Jews, the pagans were so called either from 'pagus', that is, a place, or from a single province, or from a king Paganus, which has been shown to be true, as the Greek poet Hesiod says. If, then, [the name comes] from 'pagus', it indicates a place, just as even now one says 'from that pagus'; but if from idols, *** because those who worshipped those carved images were so named pagans, that is, gentiles.
passages.notes: The text is corrupt: the stray characters after 'de pago illo' are probably scanning debris, and the edition marks a lacuna with ***. The attribution to Hesiod and the king 'Paganus' are the author's own claims.

passages.original: Certa autem est probatio et maior, quod ipsi pagani in suis historiis referunt, quod a Pagano rege, ut ait Hesiodus Grecus poeta, pagani sunt appellati: qui postea ex rege Pagano, Deucalionis filio et Pyrrae, quasi plausibile atque amabile nomen eius habentes, immo potius colentes memoriam eius usque in hodiernum diem, hoc mendacium nominis usque nunc detinent percolentes.
passages.english: But there is a sure and greater proof, which the pagans themselves report in their histories: that the pagans were named from King Paganus, as the Greek poet Hesiod says; who afterwards, [named] from King Paganus, son of Deucalion and Pyrrha, holding his name as if pleasing and lovable, or rather cherishing his memory down to the present day, still keep up and cultivate this false name to this day.
passages.notes: The etymology from a 'King Paganus' son of Deucalion and Pyrrha is not otherwise known; no such figure is identifiable in Hesiod. The syntax of the second clause is loose.

passages.original: Idola etenim, id est formas sculptilium, hominum postea pessima uoluntas inuenit. Linguam autem Grecam prouinciae unius proprietas declarauit, quam rex paganus ex suo nomine confirmauit, ut Romanos Romulus nuncupauit et ut ait Hesiodus a Greco rege fuisse Grecos appellatos, qui Grecus nomine filius fuit Deucalionis.
passages.english: For idols, that is, the forms of carved images, the most wicked will of men devised later. The particular character of a single province gave rise to the Greek language, which a pagan king established from his own name, just as Romulus named the Romans, and as Hesiod says that the Greeks were called after a king Graecus, who, Graecus by name, was the son of Deucalion.
passages.notes: 'declarauit' is literally 'made clear, declared'. The sense of the second sentence is uncertain.

passages.original: ut et Democritus ille, qui multos mundos esse adseruit, deque sua sapientia cum hoc praedicat, multorum animas sensusque dubios diuersis erroribus concitauit.
passages.english: so also that Democritus, who asserted that there are many worlds and proclaims this out of his own wisdom, stirred up the souls and wavering minds of many with various errors.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence ('ut et'), so the comparison depends on lost preceding text.

passages.original: Si quid autem falsitate Grecorum putatur esse antiquum, temporale modis omnibus ipsorum auctoribus testantibus conprobatur, Solone testante Atheniensibus quod! ab Aegyptio audierit sacerdote dicente ei:
passages.english: But if anything is thought, through the falsehood of the Greeks, to be ancient, it is proved in every way to be of [limited] time, as their own authors testify, Solon testifying to the Athenians that he had heard from an Egyptian priest, who said to him:
passages.notes: "quod!" has a stray exclamation mark, probably a scanning error, and has been read as "quod" ("that"). "temporale" ("temporal, belonging to time") is set against "antiquum" and is taken to mean "recent, not truly ancient".
